Family Health

Breast cancer in men: changes worth getting checked

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A new chest lump, nipple discharge or persistent skin change deserves a medical check. Breast cancer in men is uncommon, and many changes have other causes, but rarity is not a reason to ignore a symptom. Here is what to notice and what the next steps may involve.

Uncommon does not mean impossible

Men have breast tissue and can develop breast cancer. The disease is uncommon, which can make a new chest lump easy to dismiss or uncomfortable to discuss. A breast or nipple change deserves medical assessment even if you have never thought of breast cancer as something that could affect you.

For context, the American Cancer Society reports that fewer than 1% of breast cancers in the United States occur in men, with an average lifetime risk of about 1 in 755. Diagnosis is more common later in life, often between ages 60 and 70, but younger people can also be affected. These are population estimates, not a way to rule cancer in or out for an individual.

Information often uses the term male breast cancer because that is how studies and services describe it. Your own assessment should consider the breast tissue you have, previous surgery, hormones, family history and symptoms, alongside respectful discussion of your gender and preferences. Nobody should be discouraged from reporting a change because of a label.

Lumps and changes in the breast, armpit or collarbone area

A new lump or thickened area in the breast or chest is an important reason to book an appointment. It may be near or behind the nipple. Some cancers feel firm, irregular or relatively fixed and may be painless, but no single texture, shape or degree of movement can confirm a diagnosis.

A lump does not have to match every description in a checklist before it is worth checking. A painful or movable lump also needs assessment when it is new or unexplained. Do not wait for it to become larger, harder or sore before seeking advice.

A swelling in the armpit or near the collarbone may involve a lymph node. There are several possible causes, and it is not necessarily a breast tumour in that location. Mention it along with any chest or nipple changes so the clinician can examine the relevant areas.

Nipple and skin symptoms also matter

Look out for a nipple that newly turns inward, changes shape or develops a persistent rash or sore. Fluid coming from a nipple, including clear or blood-stained discharge, should be discussed with a clinician. You do not need to squeeze the nipple to produce discharge or repeatedly test whether it is present.

Other changes include dimpling or puckering, thickened or scaly skin, redness or swelling, an ulcer that does not heal, or a new difference in the size or shape of one side of the chest. Persistent pain at or around the nipple can also warrant a check.

These symptoms can have non-cancerous causes. That is a reason to get a proper assessment, not to diagnose yourself from a photograph. Note when the change began and whether it is progressing; describing that clearly is more useful than deciding at home whether the skin or lump “looks like cancer”.

Breast enlargement and other explanations

Gynecomastia is an increase in glandular breast tissue. It can affect one side or both, and can be tender. Hormonal changes, medicines and some medical conditions can be involved. It is not the same thing as breast cancer, although a new or changing area still needs appropriate assessment.

Other possible explanations for a lump or discomfort include cysts, infection or changes after an injury. A clinician may be able to identify a benign cause, but a self-examination cannot reliably distinguish all of these conditions.

Enlargement on both sides does not make every new symptom harmless, and a one-sided enlargement does not automatically mean cancer. Tell the clinician about medicines, supplements and hormone treatment, but do not stop prescribed treatment on your own while trying to explain the change.

Age, family history and other risk factors

Risk increases with age. A close relative with breast cancer and inherited variants such as BRCA2 (and, to a lesser extent, BRCA1) can also be relevant. Changes in genes that control cell growth may be inherited or occur during life; for many people, there is no single identifiable reason why cancer developed.

The source of a hormone change matters. Conditions such as Klinefelter syndrome, some testicular conditions or previous removal of the testes, and severe liver disease can affect the balance of estrogen and androgens. Previous radiation treatment to the chest and some estrogen treatments may also influence risk.

Excess body weight is associated with increased risk, but it is not a diagnosis or a reason to blame someone for cancer. Gynecomastia itself should not be described as breast cancer or automatically treated as a precancerous change. Some underlying conditions can be associated with both breast enlargement and cancer risk.

Having a risk factor does not make cancer inevitable, and having no known risk factor does not exclude it. A list of risks cannot tell you what a new lump is. It can help the clinician decide whether genetic advice or a longer-term screening plan is appropriate.

Symptoms elsewhere in the body

When breast cancer spreads, symptoms depend on the area affected. Persistent bone pain, breathlessness, unexplained weight loss, marked fatigue, yellowing of the skin or eyes, or a general feeling of being unwell can be reasons for medical assessment. These symptoms have many possible causes and are not proof of advanced breast cancer.

Do not wait for general symptoms before having a breast change checked. Conversely, if you already have a cancer diagnosis, tell the team about new persistent symptoms rather than assuming they are part of treatment or ordinary ageing. Sudden severe breathing difficulty, collapse or another severe acute symptom needs emergency care.

An individual outlook depends on the diagnosis, stage and treatment response. Dividing the number of annual deaths by the number of new diagnoses does not show the chance that a newly diagnosed person will die of the disease; these are different groups measured in a particular year.

What happens when you have a change assessed

A clinician will ask about the change, your health and family history, and may examine the chest and nearby lymph nodes. You can request a chaperone or ask about having a support person present. Being referred urgently to a breast clinic means the concern needs timely investigation; it does not mean that cancer has already been confirmed.

Assessment can include a mammogram, ultrasound or a needle biopsy, depending on the findings. A biopsy examines a tissue sample and can provide information about the tumour if cancer is present. You may not need every possible test.

Ask when and how results will be communicated, and who to contact if they have not arrived. If a lump changes while you are waiting, or a symptom persists after an initial reassuring assessment, tell the team. A clear follow-up plan helps prevent uncertainty from turning into a long delay.

Cancer type, receptors and stage

Invasive ductal carcinoma is the most common type of breast cancer in men. It begins in the ducts and has grown into surrounding tissue. Invasive lobular carcinoma starts in milk-producing lobules, which are usually sparse or absent in male breast tissue, so this type is rare.

Ductal carcinoma in situ, or DCIS, means abnormal cancer cells remain inside the ducts without invading surrounding tissue. It is often called non-invasive or stage 0 breast cancer and still needs a specialist treatment discussion. Calling it simply a harmless precancer would be misleading.

Many male breast cancers are sensitive to hormones. Testing the tissue for estrogen and progesterone receptors and HER2 helps guide treatment. Stage describes the extent of cancer; grade describes how abnormal the cells look. These findings are more informative for treatment planning than the outward size of a lump alone.

Treatment and inherited-risk assessment

Treatment is tailored to the cancer and the person. Surgery may remove the tumour or breast tissue, with assessment of lymph nodes when appropriate. Radiotherapy treats a defined area, while chemotherapy and other medicines may treat cancer cells throughout the body. Not everyone needs every treatment.

For hormone receptor-positive disease, endocrine treatment such as tamoxifen may be recommended. Targeted medicines depend on tumour features and the clinical situation. The choice and sequence take account of stage, receptors, overall health, other medicines, potential benefits, side effects and your preferences. A general article cannot select a regimen for you.

ASCO recommends offering genetic counselling and testing for inherited cancer-risk variants to all men diagnosed with breast cancer. Results may affect treatment or future screening and can have implications for relatives. A genetics professional can explain what a result means before family members make testing decisions.

Support also matters. Ask about body-image concerns, sexual health, side effects, work or caring responsibilities, and support services that are comfortable for you. Breast cancer care should address your life as well as the tumour.

Breast awareness is different from screening

Know what is usual for your chest. You can notice changes while washing, dressing or looking in a mirror, including around the nipple and towards the armpit. There is no need to use force, repeatedly press a sore area or squeeze the nipples. A normal-feeling self-check cannot guarantee that no cancer is present.

A fixed monthly self-examination routine is not a substitute for care, and it should not be presented as a proven screening programme for every man. Screening means testing people who do not have symptoms; investigating a new lump or discharge is diagnostic care and should not wait for a screening invitation.

People with inherited risk or a personal history of breast cancer may need a specialist surveillance plan. Ask about your own risk and which checks are appropriate locally. If you notice a new or unexplained change, make the appointment even if breast cancer feels unlikely or the conversation feels awkward.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

NHS guidance recommends assessment of new breast/chest lumps, discharge and unexplained nipple or skin changes. Symptoms do not establish the diagnosis; imaging and tissue testing may be needed.

Cancer type, stage and receptor results guide treatment. ASCO’s male breast cancer guideline also recommends genetic counselling and germline testing after diagnosis; AI editorial review is not oncology approval.

How BeMama can help

Use the guide to organise the changes you have noticed and questions about assessment or family history. BeMama cannot identify cancer from symptoms, a photograph or a self-check.

When to seek help

Arrange a prompt clinical appointment for a new breast or armpit lump, spontaneous nipple discharge or persistent nipple/skin change. Seek emergency care for severe acute symptoms such as major breathing difficulty or collapse.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Men can develop breast cancer, although it is uncommon.
  • A lump need not be painless, fixed or irregular to deserve assessment.
  • Gynecomastia and other benign conditions can cause changes, but self-checking cannot reliably distinguish them.
  • Symptoms need diagnostic assessment; screening plans are a separate discussion.
  • Treatment and inherited-risk advice are individual, and support should include the whole person.

Frequently asked questions

Can men get breast cancer without a family history?

Yes. A family history or inherited variant can raise risk, but cancer can occur without either being known. New symptoms still need assessment.

Does a painful lump mean it cannot be cancer?

No. Pain does not reliably rule cancer out, and a painless lump is not automatically cancer. A clinician should assess a new or unexplained lump.

Is swelling near the armpit the same as a breast tumour?

Not necessarily. It may involve a lymph node or another structure and can have several causes. Mention its location and any associated chest or nipple changes at the appointment.

Should I squeeze the nipple to check for discharge?

No. Report discharge you have noticed, especially if spontaneous or blood-stained. Repeated squeezing is not a reliable cancer test and can irritate the area.

Can gynecomastia affect only one side?

Yes. It can affect one side or both. That pattern alone cannot establish the cause of a new change, so seek assessment rather than assuming it is harmless or cancerous.

Do the lifetime-risk statistics tell me what my lump is?

No. Population risk describes groups over time. It cannot diagnose a symptom or replace a personal assessment.

Will an urgent referral mean I definitely have cancer?

No. It means the symptom needs timely investigation. Examination, imaging and sometimes biopsy help determine the cause.

Can men have mammograms?

Yes. Mammography may be part of a breast assessment in men, alongside ultrasound or biopsy when indicated. The team chooses tests based on the findings.

Does every man need a monthly self-exam and screening scan?

No universal scan or formal self-examination programme fits everyone. Be aware of your usual chest appearance and feel, report changes, and discuss specialist surveillance if you have inherited risk or a previous diagnosis.

Why is genetic testing discussed after a diagnosis?

An inherited variant may affect treatment, future screening and advice for relatives. ASCO recommends offering counselling and germline testing to all men diagnosed with breast cancer; the genetics team explains the choices and implications.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
